clue.text: Anger at being skint for commission

indicators.note: the phrase places the word for anger after the word for skint, as cause following feeling

parts.note: skint is British slang for having no money, i.e. broke
anger is rage

explanation.surface: Someone is furious about having no money and wants paying for their services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anger at being skint' reads naturally as RAGE at being BROKE; the answer runs the two the other way round, BROKE then RAGE. Skint is British slang for penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: A broker's fee for arranging a sale is a commission, the percentage taken for the deal.

clue.text: Is stimulated to do something about religious work?

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word meaning about or concerning
the Acts of the Apostles is a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A question whether someone is roused to activity by a work of religion.
explanation.definitionFit: To respond to a stimulus is to answer it with some behaviour, so one who is stimulated to act responds.

clue.text: What the penitent monk does when told to scrub the floor

definitions.text: What the penitent monk does when told to scrub the floor

parts.words: What the penitent monk does when told to scrub the floor
parts.note: a monk at prayer gets down on his knees, and so does anyone scrubbing a floor by hand

explanation.surface: A monk doing penance is ordered to clean the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Both praying in penitence and scrubbing a floor put a person down on bended knee.

clue.text: Ominous noise made by a doctor breaking a regulation

indicators.note: the doctor breaks into the regulation, splitting it open to sit inside

parts.note: a regulation is a rule
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A doctor flouting the rules causes a threatening stir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' looks like a doctor breaking the law, but it puts MB inside RULE.
explanation.definitionFit: Distant thunder or a growling stomach makes a low, threatening rolling sound of this kind.

clue.text: See that nothing is lost in the telling?

definitions.text: See that nothing is lost in the telling?

parts.words: See that nothing is lost in the telling
parts.note: making sure no part of a story drops out means telling everything, every particular included

explanation.surface: Advice to make sure a story keeps all its parts when it is passed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Recounting every particular of an account leaves nothing out, so none of it is lost.

clue.text: Capable of coming up with an unprecedented idea

definitions.text: Capable of coming up with an unprecedented idea

parts.words: Capable of coming up with an unprecedented idea
parts.note: a person able to think of something new is creative and original

explanation.surface: A description of someone able to have a brand-new idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Being able to devise something never thought of before is the mark of an original, creative mind.

clue.text: Home base for a growing labour force

definitions.text: Home base for a growing labour force

parts.words: Home base for a growing labour force
parts.note: 'growing' means raising crops, so the labour force is farm workers and their home base is the dwelling on the farm

explanation.surface: Headquarters for an expanding workforce, perhaps a trade union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growing' suggests a workforce getting bigger; it means workers who grow crops.
explanation.definitionFit: The main dwelling on a farm is where the farmer and hands who raise crops are based.

clue.text: Curates, long dust, will come and go On lissom, clerical, toe" (Brooke: The Old Vicarage, Grantchester)

definitions.text: Curates, long dust, will come and go On lissom, clerical, toe" (Brooke: The Old Vicarage, Grantchester)

parts.words: Curates, long dust, will come and go On lissom, clerical, toe" (Brooke: The Old Vicarage, Grantchester)
parts.note: a missing-word quotation: Rupert Brooke's poem describes ghostly curates whose light step leaves no mark, and the gap before 'toe' takes the missing adjective

explanation.surface: A line from Rupert Brooke's poem about Grantchester, near Cambridge, with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in the quoted couplet from Brooke's The Old Vicarage, Grantchester; the dead curates walk so lightly they leave no footmark.
explanation.definitionFit: The ghostly clergy tread without leaving any footmark, so their toes leave no impression.

clue.text: Not just a medley of fun and song

indicators.note: a medley is a mixture, so the letters of fun are jumbled

parts.note: an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A mix of fun and singing is described as not just anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a medley of' scrambles FUN to UNF, then AIR is added. 'Not just' looks like 'not only' but means not fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unjust is unfair, lacking fairness or equity.

clue.text: Went on board, maybe, and swapped addresses?

definitions.meaning: a player who moves a piece on a chess or draughts board has taken a turn
someone who changes home address has relocated

explanation.surface: Someone took a turn at chess, or moved house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'board' suggests boarding a ship; it is a games board.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a turn in a board game and relocating house are both described by the phrase for shifting position.

clue.text: First principle followed by an inhabitant of Central Europe

indicators.note: the first piece is placed before the second, which follows it

parts.note: a germ is the seed or rudimentary beginning of something

explanation.surface: A basic idea, then a person from the middle of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Germany, which lies at the heart of Europe, is one of its nationals.

clue.text: Art that displays no humanity

parts.note: a painting of fruit, flowers or other objects has no people in it, so it shows no humanity

explanation.surface: A complaint about art that lacks human warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints '10' where the setter wrote 'no'. 'humanity' suggests compassion; here it means people, absent from a picture of objects.
explanation.definitionFit: A painting of inanimate objects such as fruit and vases contains no human figures.

clue.text: Region of grouse moors where everyone swallows hot soup

indicators.note: the word for everyone takes the other letters inside, as a mouth takes in food

parts.note: everyone is all

indicators.note: in the soup is a mess, so soup signals the letters of hot rearranged

explanation.surface: A grouse-shooting area where all the visitors drink hot soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soup' makes THO from HOT, which goes inside ALL. ATHOLL is a district of Perthshire in the Scottish Highlands, known for grouse shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland district in Perthshire is famous for heather moorland where grouse are shot.

clue.text: Coming to a very sober con-elusion

parts.note: TT, teetotal, describes someone who drinks no alcohol at all
a conclusion is an ending

explanation.surface: Someone arriving at a very serious decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming to' looks like reaching a decision; 'Coming' alone is the definition and 'to' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being present at an event, as in coming to a meeting, is going along to it.

clue.text: They advance good reasons for raising the standard of living

definitions.text: They advance good reasons for raising the standard of living

parts.words: They advance good reasons for raising the standard of living
parts.note: the standard of living here is ethical conduct, and those who argue for better conduct are preachers of ethics

explanation.surface: Economists argue for raising people's income and comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standard of living' suggests wealth; it means the moral quality of how people live.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who urge others toward virtuous behaviour preach ethical principles.

clue.text: Slap-up tomb for a noble 11

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is read upwards, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a tomb is a grave

explanation.surface: A lavish burial place for an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slap-up' looks like 'lavish'; 'up' turns SLAP into PALS. 11 refers to the answer at 11-across, so the definition is a German noble.
explanation.definitionFit: A count palatine in the Holy Roman Empire held a German title of nobility.

clue.text: A pound put on for service?

parts.note: lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight

explanation.surface: Someone gaining a pound to be fit for military service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' suggests weight gained; it means worn. The vestment is a white linen robe worn by clergy at church services.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest dons the white ankle-length vestment before celebrating Mass or another service.

clue.text: Bit of publicity that leads to nothing but trouble

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second, leading the way to it

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a piece of publicity
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A piece of publicity that causes only trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Fuss and bother, as in much fuss about nothing, is trouble.

clue.text: Retirement for which a teacher may qualify?

definitions.meaning: retiring for the night means going to sleep in one

definitions.text: for which a teacher may qualify?
definitions.meaning: the Bachelor of Education degree qualifies a teacher

explanation.surface: Asking whether a teacher has earned their retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retirement' suggests leaving work; here it is going to sleep. The Bachelor of Education is a British teaching degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Going off to sleep is retiring for the night; a Bachelor of Education is a teaching degree.

clue.text: What seven lads do if ordered to make amphorae, for instance

indicators.note: ordered means arranged into a new order, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A question what a group of seven young men would do if told to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if ordered' looks like giving the lads a command; it rearranges WHAT SEVEN LADS DO.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphora is an ancient jar with a pair of handles, so it is an example of such a vessel.

clue.text: Not even a fraction of the harm Herod did

indicators.note: only a part of the words is taken, the run of letters sitting inside them

explanation.surface: Herod's slaughter of children was not even a fraction as bad as described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a fraction of' takes letters inside 'herOD Did'. 'Not even' means not divisible by two.
explanation.definitionFit: A number that is not divisible by two, such as three, is the opposite of an even one.

clue.text: Two cardinals, after turning pale, quietly pass away

indicators.note: the cardinal points follow the turned word
turning the word around means reading its letters backwards

parts.note: S and E, south and east, are two cardinal points of the compass

explanation.surface: Two senior churchmen go pale and die peacefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cardinals' suggests churchmen; they are compass points, S and E. 'turning' makes ELAP from PALE. 'pass away' suggests dying; it means time passing.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that slips by unnoticed is said to go by, as when years go by quietly.

clue.text: Decide not to ask for terms?

definitions.meaning: to decide a matter is to resolve or determine it
paying a bill in full rather than buying on credit terms

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to accept without negotiating conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terms' suggests negotiated conditions; it means credit terms, the alternative to paying up at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Resolving a question means determining it; paying off an account in full means clearing it without credit.

clue.text: Attitude of one who is out at elbows

definitions.text: Attitude of one who is out at elbows

parts.words: Attitude of one who is out at elbows
parts.note: out at elbows usually means shabby, but here the elbows stick out, with hands on hips

explanation.surface: Describing the outlook of someone poorly dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out at elbows' is an idiom for shabby clothes worn through; read literally the elbows stick outwards. 'Attitude' means bodily posture.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing with hands on hips and elbows pointing outward is a pose with arms bent wide.

clue.text: Certainly it could be denied

indicators.note: the letters of denied could be made into something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is certainly true, though it could be denied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it could be' rearranges DENIED. The surface plays certainty against denial.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is true emphatically, as in 'yes, truly', expresses certainty.

clue.text: Moving with indecent haste to shock the public?

definitions.text: Moving with indecent haste to shock the public?

parts.words: Moving with indecent haste to shock the public
parts.note: indecent haste usually means unseemly hurry, but here a naked runner dashes through a public place

explanation.surface: Someone rushing improperly to scandalise people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'indecent haste' means unseemly speed; here it is literal, running naked through a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Running naked through a public place, as at a sports ground, combines speed with indecency.

clue.text: Rough-riders employed in launderettes

indicators.note: rough treatment knocks the letters of riders about into a new order

explanation.surface: Tough horse riders working in coin-operated laundries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough-riders' reads as horse tamers, but 'Rough' rearranges RIDERS. A launderette is a British self-service laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: Tumble machines that dry washing are found in self-service laundries.

clue.text: Bad state of mind for decorating the home?

definitions.meaning: an ill humour or bad temper, an old sense of the word
a cheap water-based paint for walls and ceilings

explanation.surface: Being in a foul mood about redecorating the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The word also names a viral disease of dogs; here it means ill temper and a kind of wall paint.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for ill humour also names a cheap water-based paint for interior walls.

clue.text: An aboriginal quartet in neat array?

indicators.note: the Roman four sits inside the rearranged letters
to array is to set out in order, so the letters of neat are rearranged

parts.note: IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A tidy group of four Aboriginal people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'array' makes NATE from NEAT, and 'in' puts IV inside to give NAT-IV-E.
explanation.definitionFit: An aboriginal is an original inhabitant of a land, one born there.

clue.text: Radio sets designed for space travellers

indicators.note: something designed is made to a new plan, so the letters of radio sets are rearranged

explanation.surface: Radio equipment built for astronauts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'space travellers' suggests astronauts; it means rocks orbiting the Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Minor planets of rock orbit the Sun, travelling through space.
